opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, because it turned out to be one of the most important things we learned, and it's something people tend to underestimate. When you start working on learning from neural network weights, what we've called hyper-representations, the natural instinct is to grab whatever trained models you can find. But a random collection of checkpoints from the internet doesn't give you a clean learning signal. The models differ in architecture, data, training recipe and preprocessing, so it's very hard to tell what your representation is actually picking up.

So the first lesson was that you need to generate the zoo in a controlled way. We train populations of models where we deliberately vary certain factors, like the initialization seed, the hyperparameters, the activation function, the dropout, sometimes the dataset, and keep everything else fixed. Then you know what structure is in the population, and you can ask whether the representation captures properties like accuracy, generalization gap, or which hyperparameters produced a model.

The second lesson was about diversity. If all your models come from one seed or one tight hyperparameter setting, they sit in one small region of weight space and the task becomes trivial or degenerate. If you vary everything wildly, you end up with lots of models that never trained properly, and the signal gets washed out. You want enough variation that the zoo covers interesting regions of the loss landscape, but enough consistency that the models are comparable. Including several checkpoints along each training trajectory, not just the final weights, also helped a lot, because the evolution of the weights carries information.

Third, you have to take the symmetries of neural networks seriously. You can permute neurons in a hidden layer and get exactly the same function with completely different weights. A good zoo, together with the right augmentations or alignment, has to account for that, otherwise the model is learning around permutation noise. We actually found that using these symmetries as augmentations during self-supervised training was one of the things that made the representations work.

And finally, documentation and openness matter. That's part of why we released the model zoo datasets with all the metadata: training settings, performance numbers, checkpoints. If the community is going to treat weights as a data modality, we need shared, well-characterized benchmarks, the way ImageNet served computer vision. Otherwise everyone builds their own little zoo and results become impossible to compare.

r001.rationale: The response says a random or overly varied collection can produce a poor learning signal, but it does not state that increasing zoo size alone fails to improve training.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says diversity is needed, describing enough variation to cover interesting regions while keeping models comparable.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss scoring models based on whether they are parents or derived works in a lineage.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this turned out to be one of the more important and underappreciated parts of the whole research program. When we started looking at weights as a data modality, the first instinct was, well, let's just go collect a bunch of pretrained models from the internet, from Hugging Face or wherever, and treat that as our dataset. And that turns out to be a really bad idea, at least initially, because you have no control over anything. You don't know the training data, you don't know the hyperparameters, the architectures are all slightly different, and so the variation in the weights is confounded by a hundred things you can't disentangle.

So what we learned is that you really have to generate the model zoo yourself, in a controlled way, almost like you're designing an experiment. We would fix an architecture, say a small CNN, and then systematically vary things: the random seed for initialization, the learning rate, the optimizer, the dropout, the weight decay, the activation function, and of course the dataset, so MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR, and so on. And then we train hundreds or thousands of these models and, crucially, we save checkpoints along the entire training trajectory, not just the final model. That gives you a population of weights where you actually know what causes what.

There are a few things I'd highlight that we learned the hard way. One is diversity versus structure. If your zoo is too homogeneous, say you only vary the seed, then everything looks the same and there's nothing to learn. But if you vary everything at once, the structure gets washed out. So you want a design where you can isolate factors, and in some zoos we'd hold a lot fixed and vary one or two things, and in others we'd do a more uniform random sampling over the hyperparameter grid. Both are useful for different questions.

The second thing is that you want the full trajectory. Early checkpoints look very different from converged ones, and a lot of the interesting signal about generalization, about what the model is learning, lives in how the weights move, not just where they end up. If you only keep final models, you throw away a lot.

Third, and this is a subtle one, is the issue of symmetries. Neural networks have permutation symmetries, you can swap neurons within a layer and get a functionally identical network with totally different weights. If you're training something on top of those weights, a hyper-representation or a predictor of accuracy or whatever, that symmetry is either something you have to handle with the architecture of your model or with augmentation, or it's going to hurt you. Having a controlled zoo made that very visible, because you'd see models that were functionally identical scattered all over weight space.

And then the last thing is just scale and sheer data hygiene. You need enough models that whatever you're learning doesn't just memorize the zoo, you need to have held-out splits where the test models come from, say, a different seed range or a different hyperparameter region, so you're actually testing generalization to new models and not just interpolation. And you need good metadata: every model needs its training config, its test accuracy, its generalization gap, all recorded so you can use them as labels later.

So the short version is, a useful model zoo is not a scrape, it's a dataset you design. The population of models is the data, and you have to think about its distribution with the same care you'd apply to any other dataset. Once we did that, a lot of the downstream results, learning representations of weights, predicting properties from weights, even generating new weights, became much more tractable, and we eventually released those zoos so others could work with them too.

r001.rationale: The response says a homogeneous zoo offers little to learn, but it does not clearly state that increasing zoo size alone does not improve training.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says a zoo that is too homogeneous leaves nothing to learn and emphasizes designing for diversity while preserving structure.

r003.rationale: The response discusses training configurations, checkpoints, and held-out models, but not using parent-versus-derived lineage to score models for the zoo.

astra-6.text:
One thing we’ve learned is that you have to think quite carefully about what varies in your model zoo. If you train many networks with exactly the same setup and only change the random seed, you can study the variability of training, but you’re exploring a fairly narrow space. If you also vary hyperparameters, you get a richer population, and the task becomes understanding which differences in the weights actually tell you something about the models’ behavior.

But diversity alone is not enough. You also need useful models. A zoo dominated by networks that failed to train can make predicting accuracy look easy: you’re mostly distinguishing successful training from failure. Distinguishing among models that all perform reasonably well is a much more interesting test.

And then there’s how you split the data. If you have multiple checkpoints from one training run, you need to keep them together. Otherwise, you can end up testing on something very close to what you trained on. So the useful zoo is really the one whose variation and evaluation setup match the kind of generalization you want to study.

r001.rationale: The response says varying only random seeds explores a narrow space, but does not state that increasing zoo size alone fails to improve training.

r002.rationale: It explains that changing only random seeds yields a narrow space and that varying hyperparameters creates a richer population, communicating the need for model diversity.

r003.rationale: The response discusses keeping checkpoints from the same training run together, but does not use parent-versus-derived lineage as a scoring factor.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing we’ve learned is that the composition of the model zoo really matters. It’s tempting to say, “Let’s collect as many networks as possible,” but the more useful question is: What variation do those networks capture, and what do we want to learn from it?

If all the models come from almost identical training runs, there may not be enough diversity. But if you mix completely different architectures and tasks, you can introduce differences that overwhelm the signal you care about. So a useful starting point is a controlled zoo: keep the architecture fixed, and vary things like initialization, hyperparameters, and training progress.

You also have to think about selection bias. If you retain only the best-performing models, you lose much of the information about what distinguishes successful training from unsuccessful training. For predicting performance, that range can be very useful. For generating good models, you may want to emphasize the stronger examples.

So there isn’t one universally useful model zoo. Its usefulness depends on the downstream question and whether the variation in the zoo actually helps you answer it.

r001.rationale: It says collecting as many networks as possible is not the useful question; the zoo’s composition and variation matter.

r002.rationale: It explains that nearly identical training runs may lack enough diversity and recommends varying initialization, hyperparameters, and training progress.

r003.rationale: It does not mention a model’s derivation lineage or use parent-versus-derived status to score models for the zoo.
